utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and Your Honours. Douglas Stringer appearing with my colleague Alexis Demirdjian; intern, Antonio Garza; and Case Manager, Thomas Laugel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If there is nothing else. Yes, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That is good afternoon indeed. It is good to see some familiar faces in the courtroom. Before we bring in the next witness, Mr. Savic, I'd just like to raise a preliminary matter. When the Trial Chamber ruled upon the Rule 92 ter motion in relation to Mr. Savic, if you will remember, there were a number of associated exhibits, two of which at the time were not yet on the Rule 65 ter list of exhibits. Those two exhibits were added in our -- well, we proposed them in our second motion, and you ruled on the 19th of October in your decision that these documents were admitted on the Rule 65 ter list. Just for the record, these are 65 ter 5866, and 5867. So just for the sake of completeness, I just wanted to put that on the record, that when we will be tendering these associated exhibits, these two will be tendered, and they are now according to your ruling on the Rule 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And that is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness be escorted in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness. Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. First of all, do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please tell us your name, your date of birth, and your ethnicity, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Borivoje Savic, 2nd of February, 1949. I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are about to read the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out that the solemn declaration that you are about to make does expose you to the penalties of perjury should you give misleading or untruthful evidence to this Tribunal. Would you now read the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: BORIVOJE SAVIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Savic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, it is correct to say that you have given statements to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2002 and 2003?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You testified in the case against Stanisic and Simatovic in the year 2009?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: During the course of this summer, in July and August, you met with members of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And as a result of these meetings, a new statement was prepared for the purposes of this trial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: At this time could I ask for 65 ter 05868 to be displayed on the screen. That is tab 71, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, do you recognise the cover page of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can we scroll to the bottom of this statement in the B/C/S version, all the way down. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And at the bottom left corner, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And could we go to page 2, please, in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, on this second page and every other following page, I believe that your signature appears also at the bottom; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can we go to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: At the top of the last page, Mr. Savic, do we also see your signature under the Witness Acknowledgement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, before signing this statement, were you given an opportunity to read this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And before signing this statement, were you given an opportunity to make amendments to the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did make some changes. Minor ones, names and just some details.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And when you arrived in The Hague yesterday, were you given a copy of this statement to read once more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did get it, yes, and I did read it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, with regards to the answers recorded in your statement, would you give the same answers in the courtroom should you be asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time may I ask to tender 65 ter 05868, which is the statement, the 92 ter statement of Mr. Savic, as well as the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It should be assigned Exhibit P50. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And I assume that the associated exhibits will receive their numbers in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The memo will be circulated later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, in addition to your statement, I have some additional questions in relation to topics that are in your statement. Now, as I explained to you before, you can assume that the parties and the Judges have read your statement. Therefore, when I ask you additional questions, you don't need to give us the entire context, but you can restrict yourself to the specific question. Now, in your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Witness -- Mr. Savic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to hear it a little better. Can I have it a little bit louder, the sound. [In English] Okay. Okay. [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Savic, in the initial part of your statement you talk about the creation of the SDS and your relationship with members of the party. I would like to show you a document which is 65 ter 2887 at tab 52. Can you see the document on the screen, on the left side of the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you -- do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. It's a list of the boards, board members, and it's something that I drafted for my own records. These were the boards that we were establishing at the local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, when you say the local level, which region specifically would that be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The local board would be a local commune or a village around Vukovar. For example, we have Vera. This is a village in the area of Vukovar, and we see the president, secretary, treasurer. Then we have Sotin, which is the next locality. These are all locations around Vukovar or it could be a local commune if we're talking about the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you told us that these were established at the local level. When was the document itself prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is from 1990-1991, as the boards were being established in order to have some sort of record and to know where the board members were. I drafted this shortly after the boards were established in order to have a record of the membership and also for purposes of documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on page 1 at the right side of the B/C/S and English versions, we see, for example, the local commune of Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In English we need to droll down a little bit, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, we see the name of the president here. Are you familiar with this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Boro Bogunovic was the president. The first president, incidentally, was Nebojsa Uvalic. However, after an intervention of some kind, Boro Bogunovic was appointed in his stead, who actually in my opinion was already a police insider. Then they said that they intended for Boro to be put there because he was better there, and then we just said, Well, you can appoint whoever you like. Do whatever you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page in the English version -- in the B/C/S version, page 2. And in the English version, that is page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in the B/C/S version on -- I believe it is on the top right-hand corner, we see the membership of the Vukovar local commune?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And is that your name there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The seventh in line is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And below that we see the village of Pacetin, and this is where -- this is Goran Hadzic's village. Could you tell us, if we scroll down a little bit in the B/C/S version, please. And in the English version we need to move to the right a little bit. Very well. First of all, are you familiar with the second name, Miomir Crnogorac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am, yes. Miomir Crnogorac was from Pacetin. He lived there, and he was a member of the Pacetin board.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did Mr. Crnogorac later on occupy any functions in the SBWS government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was from Western Srem. I think that he was a minister of energy or commerce, more or less that. I don't know if it was commerce or energy. I don't know which ministry, but he was in the board -- in the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And still under Pacetin, we see two persons bearing the last name Hadzic. Are these related to Mr. Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are a number of Hadzic families in Pacetin. Goranka Hadzic is Goran's sister. Slobodan Hadzic, I think they just have the same last name, but they're not related. So it's only Goranka, and she was Goran's sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And just to clarify matters here, Goran Hadzic himself does not appear on this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Goran Hadzic was the president of the Municipal Board, so there was no need for him to be a member of the board in Pacetin. It's a different case with me. In Vukovar, people simply did not dare join in, get involved in the party work, so in my local commune, in order to fill in the required numbers, I was a member of the board. There's only that difference, excuse me. In the villages the situation was quite different. People were more free, and it was more simple to establish the boards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask for this document to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2887 shall be assigned Exhibit P51. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in relation to Goran Hadzic himself, in your statement at paragraph 22, you explain that you knew him through his father and that your wife was a teacher in the village of Pacetin. Could you tell the Trial Chamber how long have you known Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since his high school days. I think that in that period he was a pupil in the Vinkovci gymnasium. So maybe he was 17 or 18 years old. So that's since when I've known him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And how would you describe the relationship between your families?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was good. We respected one another. We got on well together. Our relations were quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Before getting involved in politics in the early 1990s, was Goran Hadzic involved in any organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, and he was elected in the 1991 elections for a deputy -- as a deputy of the Vukovar Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And in 1990 when he joined the SDS party, could you tell the Court what was the level of his education?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had graduated from the high school in Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge did he obtain any other degrees later on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's fine. Now, at paragraph 62 of this statement, you start describing the events that happened at the Plitvice Lake on the 31st of March, 1991, and that you were detained for about three days during this arrest, which also involved Mr. Hadzic. Now, you discuss at paragraph 70 of your statement how your ties with Mr. Hadzic were broken after the Plitvice incident and that he came under the influence of Milosevic following these events. I would like to show you a video, and this is 65 ter 4 -- sorry, 4809. It is listed at tab 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And for the interpreters the video bears the ERN V000-1388. Now, Your Honours, this clip lasts seven or eight minutes and we'll see how long we need it. Okay it's 65 ter 4809.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, first of all, Mr. Savic, do you recognise the speaker?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] As a president of the Municipal Board which you belong to, it is my duty to say something about our Vukovar Municipal Board even though there are many topics we are going to discuss later on. Our party was established on 10th of June last year in Vukovar and 19 boards had been established since then. Today the party has 21 boards and I congratulate you on establishing your two local boards. We have faced many problems in our party. You are familiar with them and you know who caused them. However, we managed to get over them and we should thank our current leadership for uniting us and helping us achieve unity. We are stronger and united now. As a people we have never looked to God, not left to right. We always knew that we were stronger together and we have relied on that. That's why we always sang that song 'We are stronger together.' I would like to tell you now something about the programme that we discussed at the beginning. As you know, at our rallies our main goal was united Yugoslavia, united Yugoslav People's Army. These are our goals even today. We have remained on the path of St. Sava, and I wish you all the best for this holiday today."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just pause here for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Savic, first of all, we heard Goran Hadzic say here that local boards were created in -- last year. So which date would you say this video was recorded roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: January 1971. This was St. Sava's day, and when I look at it more carefully, I think that this is Borovo Naselje settlement and the forming of the board, and I can see that he's talking about two boards in the same day. We would establish two or three boards in the same day depending on the preparations. Then we would implement that immediately. I think that this is Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I think there may be a little error in the transcript at page 11, line 25. It reads January 1971. Is that what you said, Mr. Savic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, January 1971. This is what I said. If we're talking about a year. Since the establishment, then that would be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry, it's the 1971 that I'm having a hard time with. Is that the right year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, now I'm confused. If it was St. Sava's day, then it was January. Then it must be 1971, 1971. 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for clarifying that, because --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Let's carry on here. So you said it's Borovo Naselje, January 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] As our great Serbian academician, Matija Beckovic, would say, 'St. Sava walked the path and everyone barked at him, but let's not forget that. Let's follow his road.' It is not the time to talk about the organisation of the party and its work right now. I would rather say a few words about our current problems, because I think that it is not the time for big speeches. We Serbs from Croatia are free-thinking democrats by conviction. We even had radicals before the war here, but where are we now? We found ourselves in a situation where we have to split into two parties due to the politics of one nation, to divide into Serbs and Croats. For us as people, it comes as a shock. We're not nationalists. Our views are broader, and we have to accept this as a fact and organise ourselves. I believe and I'm sure that everyone who watched TV two nights ago felt the same as me. This is what I think. Not even 80.000 Serbs could we manage to find in the world and persuade them to talk badly about other people. And others have 80.000 machine-guns in their possession ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm stopping the video here for a second. What do we see here on this image?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is this image and underneath the image we can see the writing St. Sava.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] 80.000 machine-guns in their possession and they keep them so they could use them against us. It's ridiculous. 1941 happened and 1941 happened -- 1945 happened too. Then in 1971, we thought we would forgive them. It would never happen again. But I'm telling you now ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you recognise some of the people we showed so far, under the flag at the desk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise Mile Vukas, who was from the local commune in Borovo. A member of the board there. I recognise some of the faces, and to my great surprise I can actually recognise myself too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Are you on this -- on this still?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's me in the middle. But I don't remember any details. There's nothing really specific that I can say apart from what we have seen and heard. This is the session at which the board was established. Judging by the clothes I'm wearing, I had just arrived. I had been underway somewhere or I was about to travel somewhere. You see that most people are wearing their everyday clothes unlike me, but it's very difficult for me to think back and recall the exact details where I'd been off to, where I'd just arrived from, or indeed where I would soon go.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Play the rest of the video here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] If the Croatian people do not publicly renounce on their Ustasha policy, we will propose through our Serbian National Council that we cut all ties between Serbs and Croats. A perfidious policy pursued since the 1850s, since the time of Ante Starcevic has now reached its final stage but they were not that perfidious. They let -- had they pursued their perfidious policy for another couple years, the Serb people would not have managed to unite. They can do nothing to us now. In the work of our party at a regional level, republican federal level, we face problems. Let me tell you why: Because we are democrats. We have not thought about things they had said and we thought whether or not they really meant it. However, I thank them for that. We are united and there will be no division within the party. We understood that people should talk to each other, but there is no dialogue with people who are not people with inhuman people. I would not discuss this anymore. I would like to invite you to join the Serbian Democratic Party instead. You don't have to become members of the party, but you have to follow its policies and participate in its activities."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, we just heard a moment ago Goran Hadzic saying that: "If the Croatian people do not renounce their Ustasha, we will propose through our Serbian National Council to cut all ties between Serbs and Croats." Now, in your statement at paragraph 132 and 133, you described the use of the word "Ustasha." Was it usual for Mr. Hadzic to use this terminology?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every now and then. Nevertheless, may I explain. These are activities that were triggered by the daily goings-on in terms of politics. When people spoke publicly, they spoke based on what they'd seen on TV, what they'd read in the papers, and so on and so forth. One had to take every opportunity to garner applause, to be publicly acclaimed. So it was a perfectly normal type of register to use when addressing an audience depending on the audience, the people who were actually there. So, yes, one tended to use that kind of expression at the time. It was very difficult to convince people. When you spoke about the Ustasha, you actually were helping the Croatian side. The Croats had their own platform. They were pursuing that platform. They were telling us openly what they would do, and we needed our own platform, too, instead of following the Croats or indeed anyone else. I myself opposed these unnecessary acrobatics and making daily political references like this during these speeches. I tried to exert my influence to keep people from using such expressions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And why would you try to influence people to keep from using such terminology?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, if you think about the idea behind the establishment of the board and the Serbian Democratic Party in this area, the idea was mine and mine alone. I tried to talk to the people in Vukovar, the whole town. I must have talked to about 300, 400 people. I informed them all about what it was that it would be doing and that we were aiming to get the party off the ground, but not a single time did I ever use the word "Serb" during my contacts with these people. But each and every one of them told me invariably, You know I'm a Serb. As soon as someone told me that, You know I'm a Serb, what that meant to me is that there was nothing more for me to expect from that particular person. I should meddle no more. I'll just try to help as much as I can. So it was all moving in that general direction. And then we started canvassing the villages around the town itself where the atmosphere prevailing there was very different and people were acting a different way. They were somehow freer, and we in turn were freer to do our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I would like to -- we can remove this clip now. I would like to show some of the stills so we could help us identify some of the people on the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen 65 ter 4809.4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before going to another topic, sorry. Mr. Savic, I would like to go back to the Ustasha terminology. If I understood you correctly, and please tell me if I did, the word "Ustasha" coming from Goran Hadzic is a pejorative term for Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. And I won't ask a second question, because I was going to ask you if at that time Croats themselves would call themselves Ustasha. Where there were Croats that would call themselves Ustasha?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The Croats were not referring to themselves as Ustasha, but I believe you've heard a lot already about the Ustasha and about the Chetniks. These were two very backward movements among the Serbs and among the Croats respectively. During the Ustasha time, half of Croatia was under Italy. The Chetnik movement in Serbia split the nation up into two halves. You had the Partisans on the one hand and the Chetniks on the other. And what this led to was a fratricidal war. So these are two backward movements politically and ideologically speaking. So the ideologues behind these movements were Communists. That's what it means. They were particularly skilful at manipulating these Ustasha and these Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. That was very clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: [In English] And just to follow up on His Honour's question, Mr. Savic, what does this speech tell us in relation to Goran Hadzic's views at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What can I say about his views? As soon as we were set up as a board, obviously there was a lot of focus on us by other services operating in the area, some legal, some illegal. Nevertheless, the ground was covered by a network of these services. Goran, nevertheless, was president, and he had a certain freedom in terms of who he was getting in touch with and how he was talking to people. At that time and while we were still primarily in the town itself, we were still quite united, as simple as that. But I was the first to fall under the influence of these services and agents operating there, but I refused to settle for any of the arrangements that were on offer, particularly those across the Danube. I can explain that, and it's simple enough really. The Serbian Democratic Party had a platform, and the platform covered the Republic of Croatia in territorial terms. We were to operate in the Republic of Croatia, and we would be a party to Croatia's parliamentary life. I did not believe that it was in our interest to link up with anyone in Serbia or any other service. It was often said that the Croat-Serb issue was the heart of the matter in terms of how the crisis might be resolved. Nevertheless, this was really an issue between Zagreb and Belgrade. That's what it was. The Serb-Croat issue was not something for the Serbs in Croatia. The Serbs in Croatia were an issue for Croatia, a democratic issue that Croatia had to come to terms with. And that, I think, is the simplest explanation if you want to understand the direction that our work as a party took at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Can you see the -- the image, going back to this video, on this screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The image might be a little bit blurry. I don't know if you can identify anybody on this picture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Mile Vukas, the man on the left at the edge of the table, who appears to be writing something. The one with the moustache. He's sitting at the edge of that table. I don't recognise the rest. Nevertheless, having watched that footage a minute ago, I caught a segment where I could recognise Vukcevic, Professor Vukcevic. And now understand one thing. Professor Vukcevic and I were off to another meeting right after this one, and that's why I was waiting for the Assembly to conclude, and I am talking of Borovo of all places.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Can we go perhaps to page 6 of this set of photos. Is this the same person you were telling us earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's Mile Vukas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have a set of eight or nine photos. Perhaps it would be useful to just identify this person with the letter A. Maybe the usher can help us marking this picture with the pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps in the top right-hand corner of this image you could write the person's name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mile Vukas; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My hand's a bit unsteady.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. If we could see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see what I wrote, can't you? My hand was at an awkward angle, but I think you can actually read what I wrote, can't you? Or perhaps you want me to write it all over again, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I think it's on the record as well as. So it'll be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we could seize image and if I could tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 4809.4, page 3 in e-court marked by the witness shall be assigned Exhibit P52. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page. I'm sorry. The next one. No. We already saw that one. And the last one, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The person to the right of this image, who would that be, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The face is familiar, but I can't remember his name. I can't remember his name. He left Vukovar, so I haven't seen him for a very long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. So you just mentioned Professor Vukcevic. We hadn't discussed him earlier. Is he in any of these images or was he in the video-clip that you saw earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did catch sight of him just very fractionally. He was to my left somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Moving on, you just mentioned the work of the party. I'd like to show you another document which is at tab 10, that is 65 ter 00102.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'm just reminded that the video-clip that we just viewed hasn't been tendered. Perhaps I could make a submission after the first break about this video, because it's about an hour, and we would be seeking to tender the entire video. So at this stage perhaps we can mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You would not be seeking --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We would be seeking to tender the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The entire.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: -- entire. Yes. It's a clip of about seven or eight minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The entire video is about an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You see. So perhaps we could mark it for identification now and I will make a submission after the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What is the 65 ter number of the entire video, Mr. Demirdjian?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The entire video is 65 ter 4809.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The Registrar tells me that they don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: They don't have the whole video. Okay for now let's just tender the clip and we'll deal with the whole video later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification or just marked?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: For admission, full admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, video-clip under 65 ter 4809.3 shall be assigned Exhibit P53. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the platform of the Serbian Democratic Party Regional Board for Slavonia and Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you say Slavonia, Baranja, does that apply to both Slavonias? Both eastern and western?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We just tried to keep it short, so we said Slavonia and Baranja, which includes both east and west. We wanted to avoid using any really long names like the Communists did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, at the top of this page we could see that it was -- it was prepared at a session of the 3rd of February, 1991, in Lipik. Could you -- just to situate ourselves could you tell the Trial Chamber where Lipik is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's right next to Pakrac. It's a thermal resort from Austro-Hungary. It's very old. So the meeting was held there because they actually have a hall that was big enough to hold all of us, all the candidates, and on the 3rd of February that was where we assembled to establish our board.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, on this page we can see that's the programme of the work of the SDS, and I'd like to bring your attention to item number 2. In the English version could we scroll down a little bit. Thank you very much. Under item 2, in the second paragraph of item 2 it is written here that: "In the present order of things and relations, any kind of contact with the party in power in Croatia is out of the question until the abolishment of the legal institutional and other norms and practices which deprive the Serbian people of their rights." Now, in what context was this issued, Mr. Savic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we were preparing for the multi-party elections in Croatia, during that time the Croatian Democratic Union was set up as a party that was meant to unite all Croats and their interests and also to articulate the interests of the Croatian people. The party was set up first and foremost in order to finish the work -- the groundwork laid by the Communists. Their approach was quite open about one thing, the Serbs in Croatia, and this was always seen as something of a problem for the Croats, the percentage of Serbs -- Serbian population in Croatia. They were loud and clear about this, that we would have our rights taken away, our property taken away, that we would be driven out and eventually liquidated. So what they ended up doing, they had been very up front about it previously. So you have to see this story against that background. First came the constitutional changes. The Serbs saw some of their rights taken away pursuant to the new constitution. People were angry and dissatisfied as they were being manipulated by both sides at the same time. So this is the background against which you must see these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 3 in the B/C/S version, and that is page 4 in the English version. Under item 7 -- in the B/C/S we need to scroll down a little bit. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, by this time, this is the 3rd of February, 1991, we see here that the SDS is working actively to establish Serbian autonomy. Was this an item that was high on the agenda already at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you know, amid all this chaos and everything that was going on, it was very difficult to prioritise. A platform and our positions really depended on how the political situation continued to evolve. Would Croatia secede and become independent? Would there be a confederation? Or would there be a third solution in terms of localising the existing crisis? No serious discussion on our political status could possibly take place. The pendulum kept swinging between political autonomy, territorial autonomy, and so on and so forth, but in practical terms it was all on a day-to-day basis and it was impossible to define what course events would take.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And who -- who received this -- this document or who was it meant -- who was it meant to be written for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document, the party platform, was drafted by Milun Karadzic, who was secretary of the Slatina board. He was very active, an elderly gentleman who tended not to move about too much, but we spent most of our time travelling around. So it was up to him to draft the platform. But it wasn't really carefully designed platform. It was just a spur of the moment thing, a sudden inspiration. We were the first movement, and then we had to set ourselves up as a proper political party. Therefore, we needed as many documents as we could possibly get and as much political material to legitimise our position as a political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And who was the document distributed to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Candidates were appointed at the Assembly meeting who were people from Municipal Boards. Mr. Hadzic from Vukovar and Mr. Bogunovic as well. A number of others, too. All of the delegates were familiar with the platform. They were shown the platform and served a copy. Milun Karadzic was in charge of the Presidency's work. I was a member of this Presidency. The entire board was familiar with this. There was another noteworthy situation. Mr. Hadzic and Mr. Bogunovic were the names put forward as members of the board. Following the Assembly meeting, I had come under a lot of pressure by Veljko Dzakula, Ilija Sasic, and someone else whose name escapes me. They wanted me to join the board as well. I said, Goran is the board president. Bogunovic has now been appointed. There's no need for me to join. Nevertheless, they were adamant that I should join as well. I'm not sure what their intentions were, but they were very unhappy about me not joining, but that's what it was. The people who were appointed eventually became board members, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could I offer this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 102 shall be assigned Exhibit P54. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, Mr. Savic, you explain how after the events at the Plitvice Lakes your ties with Mr. Hadzic were broken. Did you have any contacts with him following this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were in the prison hospital in Zagreb for two days separately. On the first day I had a meeting with Degoricija and assistant justice minister, Hajdukovic. The second day, the minister of the interior Mr. Boljkovac and his assistant came, and we agreed then that we should go home, that they would escort us. After that, I was brought home and they left me there. So we didn't have any more direct contacts for a couple of days at least. I was not free to move around. I had to be careful. I had to be careful where I went, why I went. Simply the goal was for me to be expelled from Vukovar. There was a lot of noise in the media. There was a lot of pressure. There were attacks on the house by telephone and in all other possible ways, but I stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And after your release, what happens to the -- what happened to the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many things began to change quickly after that, and things moved along quickly. I couldn't get involved with that that much anymore. All the activities were taken over by Vukasin Soskocanin within the party, who was the president of the board in Borovo. That was the biggest board that we had. From time to time they contacted me about co-ordinating activities and tasks, but within a couple of days, actually, I was told by the people from the HDZ board in Vukovar that an order had arrived about my liquidation. Why did I say the HDZ? Because very often the HDZ is discussed in a negative context as the party exclusively to blame for everything that happened. However, the Vukovar board and the people in Vukovar there, I was in very good terms with them. Even before I take over the board I contacted them. I asked them what they thought about it, and they were in favour of it. They said, Well, something has to be tried. We have to try something. So they reported to me from the board, and they said, You know that now no harm will come to you from us, but there are a lot of people who have been brought in from the outside, so just be careful where you go. After that, I was summoned by the Croatian radio Zagreb, Mirjana Rakela, the editor, called me and asked if I was willing at 1630 hundred hours on the 2nd of May to participate in a programme that would be broadcast live on radio Zagreb. I cannot remember the name of the programme anymore. And then she said, Mr. Savic, you will be broadcast live. Everything you say will be broadcast live. She was very willing to go through with this. I said, Well, I cannot tell you anything right now about this but let's talk in a couple of days, but as far as I'm concerned, there's no problem. After that -- so this was planned for the 2nd of May. So one day I received information that Mr. Hadzic was in Zagreb to see the assistant minister of the interior, Mr. Degoricija. I didn't know anything about this, so I was a little surprised about it, even though he had the right -- in any case, I think Degoricija invited him to come. Simply I was a bit reluctant. I didn't insist about anything. I didn't want to create any problems about this, particularly because there was a completely different order that had come about myself. So I then just took it a notch down about all of these activities, or I controlled myself, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to wrap up on the topic, what happened to the political activities of the SDS party during the summer of 1991? Did it continue carrying out its activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a lot of pressure already after the formation of the Serbian National Council. People were falling away. There was a parallel group of people who introduced themselves as a constituent organ. They were saying that the party could not be a constituent organ and the Serbian National Council would take over all the functions in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Moving on to a slightly different topic, at paragraph 123 of your statement, you explain that a retired JNA general, Radojica Nenezic, had recommended Goran Hadzic to Slobodan Milosevic to make him the man who would represent the SBWS. Could you tell the Court when this took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I was first offered to go to Belgrade for talks but I didn't go, but in any case, I controlled who would go and through whom this -- these contacts would proceed. So Goran proceeded in this way. We contacted. We spoke openly. We were together. We drove together a lot, and I asked him, What does it mean to get close to Milosevic in this way, and what does it mean to you to go to Belgrade? And he said to me, Well, listen. Milosevic is a true Serb. He is a good man. He doesn't have any major political ambitions. Let's just have this resolve itself and then he will step back. And it was all a lot of nonsense. I mean, I didn't really go into it whether he would stop with his activities or not. Secondly, anyone who went to Belgrade, they would always say, I'm going to see Milosevic, but the road to Milosevic through -- leads through some alternative ways, through the SPS political party or the old retired functions from the Military Intelligence Service, the KOS. So this Nenezic was a person from this area. He was quite correct in his conduct, popular among people. So at one time when we met each other during the summer and we met each other at his initiative, he told me that he regretted very much recommending Goran and for -- and I can tell you he even died with this burden. He was very unhappy and very sad that things had taken this turn. So there was this line through which probably some other people, too, did it. I mean, there were more lines to Belgrade than telephone lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm skipping a little bit ahead in time, sir, because I want to show you a video so you can help us identify a few individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could I ask for 65 ter 04982 to be played on Sanction. Okay. So that's 04982.1, and the ERN is V000-6733. We can start playing it from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you see the video on your screen, Mr. Savic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, we showed you this video yesterday. Is it correct you saw this for the first time yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And it is correct to say you're not able to identify the location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'll ask you to help us with some of the people we see on the screen. Do you recognise this person right here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What do we see behind him? What's the emblem there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that ought to be some kind of emblem with eagles. This is one of those Serbian insignia. It's some sort of Serbian insignia. I would often say that whoever would make something up, they would immediately implement it. So this is the same with this symbol. I think it says "Baranja" on it or something. There is a name on the -- on the symbol, but I cannot really tell what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says "Krajina," I think. Captain First Class Mladic. I think that the person in the glasses behind him is Frenki Simatovic in the second row. Jugoslav Kostic is in the first row. I don't know this older man next to Mladic. Vojin Susa is behind in the second row next to Frenki. Mile Paspalj, Goran Hadzic. I cannot recognise the person next to Goran. I simply don't know who that is. And here is Jaja, chief of the Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem security service, Stevo Bogic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Perhaps we could at this time pull up the stills we have from this video so you can mark the individuals with letters so we can record this. So this would be which 65 ter number? 4982.2 for the stills. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do you intend to tender only stills or the video as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In this case, Your Honour -- in this case, Your Honour, we will tender the stills. We will have another witness to identify the location and the time, et cetera. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. On this first still, maybe if you can mark the first person to the left with the letter A and tell us who that person is on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe with the assistance of the usher redo that letter A, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I know it's not very easy on the screen, but let's give it a shot again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. This is not the best thing for me. I cannot manage to do this. It's not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Would a circle work?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We will have two circles on this image, that's the problem. But we can say person to the left, person to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Who is the person on the far left in the first row? Okay. Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Goran Hadzic is on the left. That's marked by the letter A. It was supposed to be a letter A. On the right-hand side is Stevo Bogic, marked with a B. So this is not the person right next to Goran but the one -- the second person from -- standing from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can I ask for this image to be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 4982.2, e-court page 1 marked by the witness, shall be assigned Exhibit P55. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can I ask to go to the next page, please, in this set of photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. And can you tell us in this image next to Mr. Hadzic who is the person there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mile Paspalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Can we go to the very last page, please. And I'm sorry -- how can we do this?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps we could tender the image we just saw with the comment that it's Mr. Paspalj. The whole set. Okay. Let me just deal with this one too. On this picture I would need the assistance of the usher to mark a few persons, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You already gave us some comments while watching the video. Can you mark the individuals again starting from the far left, the persons that you recognise with the letter A, B, C, and D, if possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Captain First Class Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Who else do you recognise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the person standing next to him, but the person next to that one is Jugoslav Kostic. Are we going to use A and B again?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. And for the individuals behind that you were talking about you can use the letters C and D?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Frenki Simatovic is behind, then. That's C. And Vojin Susa is D.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Can we capture this image as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Very well, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 4982.2 page 9 marked by the witness shall be assigned Exhibit P56 thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier Stevo Bogic, Mr. Jaja. To your knowledge, you already told us his function. You said he was head of the state security. Now, how long did he remain in that position, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know for how long, but I know that Goran boasted, saying that the appointment of Mr. Stevo Bogic for chief of security service would guarantee peace in the area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. That's what he said. Bogic was a problematic person, a provocateur, somebody who might even threw out from meetings, sometimes. And once at a meeting with some people were Belgrade at one time when I prompted him a little bit he said, Do you know that he threw me out of meetings? And I said, Yes. And as for you and me, nothing has changed there. I don't why Goran appointed him. I don't know what his reasons were, but there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Can I show you a document. It's at tab 38. It's 65 ter 05869. Now, you can see that this is a list. It says here "List of salary payments." On the next page in a moment we will show you the date of this document. You can see the list of members here. You have president of the republic, Goran Hadzic, and under number 7 you still see Mr. Stevo Bogic. Can we go to page 2, please. In English as well. Do you see the date on this document, Mr. Savic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The 15th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you were -- you were still in the region at the time in 1992. Does it fit with your recollection that Mr. Bogic was still a member of the government at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that he was, yes. In 1992, I was in Vukovar, in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And I apologise. Could we return to the first page. Now, you see the list of ministers and by this time I assume that this is the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I saw Knin at the bottom. I think that this would be the Knin people, because Paspalj, Zdravko Zecevic, this is all Knin. The prime minister. Paspalj was a speedily elected president of the Assembly when the Vance-Owen Plan was supposed to be signed. They brought him from the forest and appointed him to be as the president of the Assembly, because some document needed to be signed. He is a forestry engineer. Then you have Dzakula. He was the president of the municipality. I think that he was doing something in the Red Cross. That's Knin. It's Knin. Bogic, Stevo, then that's the government of the Serbian Republic of the Krajina then. Because we had so many Assemblies and governments that's now it's very difficult to tell which one is which. Then this is the Republic of the Serbian Krajina after it was formed up there in the village. Then Stevo was the chief of the security service of the Krajina then. Koncarevic, Ilija; Veljko Vukelic. I know all of these people from the list and I know where they are, but I don't know what they were doing. Well, here the secretary of the government, Dusan Starovic, Jelica Radmila, secretary of the Assembly but this is the government of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May I offer this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Before we take the break -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 5869 shall be assigned Exhibit P57. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just before we take the break, Your Honours, can I clarify one answer the witness just gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned that Paspalj was speedily elected president of the Assembly when the Vance-Owen Plan was supposed to be signed. Is that correct? Is that what you meant by it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Babic was against that. He didn't want to sign it. I don't know exactly what this was about, but anyway, that was the principle of how they resolved problems, to find somebody from the area, no matter who, no matter what, and then if they appointed -- if they agreed and were appointed, if a signature was necessary, then they would immediately proceed towards appointing that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And I just wanted to clarify. For the plan, you said Vance-Owen. Is that the right name of the plan? Because we're in 1992 here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of the peace agreements. Don't hold me exactly to the word. I mean I just said Vance-Owen like that. It was one of the peace agreements that was used then as a pretext to appoint Paspalj as the president of the Assembly and the Vance-Owen Plan was not there in 1991. That's -- that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Maybe this is an appropriate time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: How long will you need after the break, Mr. Demirdjian?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I have one video and two maps to show, so I would expect about 15 minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, we'll take -- Mr. Savic, we'll take the break now and come back at 3.30. You will be escorted out now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can the witness be escorted in, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've been informed that I have about seven minutes left on the time we estimated, so I'll try to wrap it up as quickly as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, in your statement, at paragraph 140, you explained the organising of volunteers who were sent from Serbia to the area of Vukovar. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can I show you the next video-clip, which is 65 ter 4873.1, and the ERN is V000-2233.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Anchor: As previously announced, Goran Hadzic, president of the Serb region of Slavonia Baranja and Western Srem, is in our studio. Good evening. "Goran Hadzic: Good evening. "Anchor: When did you arrive in Belgrade? "Goran Hadzic: Well, I arrived last night. "Anchor: Can I ask you as a reporter what the current situation in the theatre of war is? "Goran Hadzic: Well, the situation is much clearer military-wise. We have a big part of free liberated territory in our area, that is the whole of Baranja, Western Srem from Vinkovci in the direction of Sid and the bigger part of this Osijek field. That is between Osijek and Vukovar. Vukovar is currently blocked. We expect denouement of the situation in Vukovar any day. We are capable of dealing with this quickly but we are thinking of human lives and taking care that this will be done slowly and securely with as few casualties as possible; that is, we do not want any casualties. "Anchor: Do you have information on events in Vukovar? Do you have information on Serb people in Zagreb?"

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I just pause it here for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Here Mr. Hadzic is mentioning that some parts of the territory is free. Vukovar is still blocked. Could you situate for the Trial Chamber around which time this interview would have taken place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This interview might have occurred just before the fighting in Vukovar ceased, which was sometime on the 18th or the 19th. So I would place this sometime back in early November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's play the rest of the clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Do you have any information on the Serb people in Zagreb? "All communications lines are down. There are no phone lines available and people cannot talk to their families. "As I said, I'm not concerned with the military issue. I am positive a final solution will follow. I am, however, concerned about some information I personally received from some of our services. They tell me what the situation is in Zagreb and we know what happened in Vukovar, mass crimes against the civilian population. We will interrogate perpetrators and bring them to face a court a law, a national court. I'm certain they will be punished accordingly for their misdeeds. It is no use whining. This is neither asked nor expected of us. The Serbs never whine. Serbs should fight and will fight to protect their people. "You have already appealed to all able-bodied men to return to their homes and join their comrades who are already on the front line. Was the appeal successful? "The appeal was success fell in every way. A number of our combatants who fled have now returned. They are now fighting along the front lines. We also called in volunteers from Serbia irrespective of their party affiliations, Serbs to join or ranks and fight with Serb insignia for the Serbian people who are at risk. They came. I will take this opportunity to thank all of them to came to fight. The group from Belgrade stands out. They are always on the first lines of combat. They fight and they are killed just like us but do not hesitate to go all the way and win."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, at this clip at the last section we hear Mr. Hadzic talking about the volunteers who joined from Serbia. Having regard to what you've said in your statement, to your knowledge who on the side of the SBWS was co-ordinating -- co-ordinating or responsible for the reception of the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence board of Vukovar was set up in Sid. This boards would spend their days registering people who came over from Vukovar to register with the board. They would give them weapons. They would give them appropriate clothes to wear, and they would take them to Vukovar. So the Territorial Defence Staff of Vukovar in Sid was in charge of doing that for everyone from -- from our area. That is from the Vukovar area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And could you tell the Trial Chamber who was in charge of this staff in Sid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Filipovic was the commander, and Slobodan Grahovac was the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And at paragraph 142 of your statement, you mentioned that Borislav Bogunovic was also at the headquarters in Sid. What was his role there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The staff was housed on the premises of the Socialist Party of Serbia in the town centre of Sid. Day-time activities proceeded as per usual. Sometimes Boro Bogunovic, Kertes and other people would visit during the times that I was there. So these, roughly speaking, would be the people who dropped by. Boro Bogunovic was minister of the interior of the Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem. I suppose that was the capacity, official capacity in which he appeared there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May I offer this video, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 4873.1 shall be assigned Exhibit P58. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The last topic that I'd like to deal with, Mr. Savic, is the issue of Lovas, where you explain in your statement that you stayed there for several weeks in October and November 1991. Now, it is correct to say you stayed there until the end of the operations in Vukovar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you indicated that you knew a number of people there, and you've indicated also a number of locations in paragraph 150 onwards of your statement. What I would like to do is mark these locations on an aerial image we will be displaying on the screen. That is 65 ter 6276 at tab 64. And with the assistance of the usher I hope we can mark some of these locations. Are you able to situate yourself on this map, Mr. Savic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: First, could you indicate with a line the main road leading into Lovas on this map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The main road leading into Lovas is on the left-hand side of the screen. So this is the main line leading all the way into Lovas town centre or village centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. In your statement you mention a police station. Are you able to locate the police station on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The police station was here, in the middle of the village. You go up to access the village, and the police station was the first building on the left. The house used to belong to someone, a person who used to work in Germany. It was a new house, well equipped. It would not have been right for the police not to enjoy an appropriate degree of comfort, would it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, I know it's a little bit difficult. Would you be able to mark it with -- let's start with number 1 this time instead of letters, see if that could make it easier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is number 1, in which case that should be over here. There's a bit of a blot here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could the usher perhaps help us clean that up and write number 1 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you just mark number 1 there without putting a line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There you go, number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Then you also mention that when the government had meetings in Lovas, they held meetings in a building next to the police station. Can you mark that with a 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was right across the way from that building. There was a residential building there containing also some business premises. It's a building that belonged to the Lovas co-op. It was right across the way. There was some separate rooms on the ground floor, and a grocery, whereas the last two floors were reserved for residential flats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You also mention that shortly after the takeover of Lovas a headquarter was established by Ljuban Devetak. Where would that be located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That building and those premises were used for the purposes of the staff as well. There was enough room there, and that building was used for everything that was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Can you say -- when you say that building, do you mean the building you marked with number 2 just now; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 2, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And are you able to locate the Zadruga building on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The workshop and the machine factory as well as the kitchen, it was down the street from that building in the opposite direction towards the lower corner of this photograph. It was right here. You can see that there are actually some hangars there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did the JNA have any headquarters in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA were using a house that is further down the street from the police station. It was here somewhere, also to the left and further down the street from that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just for the record, you've marked the JNA house with the number 4; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 4, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And again for the record, you marked the Zadruga as number 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You also mention in your statement that the JNA had a check-point at the entrance of the village. Is that visible on -- would that be visible on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be on the left-hand side of this image. So this is the start of the access road, and you can see the co-op facilities here. It's a large-scale yard. You can see a number of hangars there. There's a silo over here, and this is where the check-point was, on the -- right next to the gate that people used to access the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you mark that area with the number 5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Is that visible enough, Your Honours? Okay. Can I ask to mark this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter document 6276 marked by the witness in court shall be assigned Exhibit P59. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And my last question on this topic, at paragraph 193, you state that Goran Hadzic -- you had seen him in Lovas. Can you indicate to us how many times you had seen him in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Goran was sometimes there. We met several times, even along the access road. We would exchange greetings, that sort of thing, but I never attended any meetings there. I don't know who he was with. I suppose with Ljuban, but he would sometimes come and, yes, I did see him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just to be clear, you were there during the months of October and November? Is that -- would that be right, or can you specify how long you were in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there until the cessation of hostilities in Vukovar. As soon as one could go to Vukovar, I went immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And you told us that you didn't -- you don't know who he was with when he came to Lovas. Did you know what he was doing when he came to Lovas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I saw him, he was on his own. We met twice at the very gate. We just greet each other. He would go his way, and I would go mine. That's what happened. I never really asked any questions as to his reason for being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And you were saying that you never attended meetings there. To your knowledge were there meetings in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know there were some dinners and lunches that Ljuban organised for the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem or individual ministers. He was particularly fond of organising parties for Jaja. I don't know of any other meetings except for the 2nd of October. I think a government meeting took place on that date. I was in charge of organising that meeting. The objective of that particular meeting was for the government to show up in this area, the government from Erdut. All the people from the villages across the area were assembled. This was harvest season, but they didn't have anything to use in terms of equipment or anything like that. So we talked about the harvest mostly. That was the subject discussed at the meeting and people came from as far afield as Erdut, about seven or eight of them. If you need their names I could enumerate them for you. I think there are actually minutes from that meeting that are available somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, and those minutes are mentioned in or statement. I just want to clarify. When you say Ljuban, can you give us his last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ljuban Devetak. Whenever I say Ljuban, that's who I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's all I ask. I'm told that I have to mention something for the record in relation to the clips. If I may be given a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll deal with it after the next break just to clarify. It's in relation to the video-clips and as associated exhibits. I'll get back to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Savic, good afternoon. My name is Zoran Zivanovic and I represent Mr. Hadzic in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You answered a question by my learned friend the Prosecutor, saying that you gave two statements to the OTP, one in 2002, the other in 2003; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also testified in the Stanisic case, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Previously you had met with the Prosecutor twice in order to prepare you for your testimony in that case in 2008 and 2009, had you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Finally, we see this new consolidated statement from you which the Prosecutor has shown you and which you signed. I will be asking you a series of questions in relation to that amalgamated statement. I will tell you right off it was very difficult for me to distinguish some things based on that statement, namely the things you said which you know by means of direct knowledge, direct experience, meaning you actually heard or saw something yourself on the one hand and on the other your own views, your own positions and theories which you somehow acquired at the time.
