So it was very difficult for me as I was reading your statement to keep the two apart. Now this statement has been admitted into evidence. You make a total of 74 references to Slobodan Milosevic in that statement in a total of 39 different paragraphs of your statement. What I want to know is this: Did you ever actually meet Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You gave the first two statements in 2002 and 2003 at a time when the Milosevic trial was underway before this Tribunal. Did the OTP call you as a witness in that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I also noticed that you make several references to Vojislav Seselj in your statement, Vojislav Seselj and his acolytes or members of his party, a total of 53 references in a total of 25 different paragraphs throughout your statement. Did the OTP ever call you to appear as a witness that at that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on your testimony in the Stanisic and Simatovic trial, I noticed that you were asked an explicit question by one of the Defence counsel, I believe, and you said that you were never directly in contact with either Stanisic or Simatovic. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that, does that mean, Yes, that's true, that's what I said, or, That's true, I was never directly in contact with either of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was never directly in contact with either of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is something I'd like to ask you first just to shed light on some of your movements following the 2nd of May, 1991. I'm reading your statement and I get the impression that up until that time, the 2nd of May, you were living in Vukovar. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is the day you left for Serbia; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us exactly where you settled down when you arrived in Serbia on the 2nd of May? Where did you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Sabac, in my parents' home, also in Odzaci, in a studio that I got from the Hypol general manager, Mr. Knezevic. He allowed me to use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How long were you in Sabac for, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My mother was there and I would come and go. It's really difficult to pinpoint a time period. I would go there every couple of days, whenever I needed some rest. Whenever I needed to calm down a little, that was what I would go. So it wasn't something definite. It was whenever I needed to go, that's when I went.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you were not in Sabac all the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. Mostly I moved from Vojvodina in Backa Palanka to Apatin, Sombor. That's the area that I moved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you where you lived. Does that mean you also lived in Backa Palanka, Apatin, Sombor, in Odzaci, or you lived in a specific place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, between Backa Palanka, Odzaci, Sombor, there's only half an hour distance. When I was in my studio apartment, I was in Odzaci, and all these other places I went to on day trips.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you lived in Odzaci, and from time to time would go to visit your mother in Sabac, and you went to other places as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how long were you in Odzaci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think until late May 1991. Until the 20th of May, let's say. Then I moved to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you rent an apartment there or did you live --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Belgrade I lived either in a hotel or I would just go to Sabac. I had some sort of accommodation. I mean, we were putting up refugees in a place in Zvezdara. There was a kindergarten that we were given for our use, so very often I was up there in that kindergarten. There were dorms that were prepared for refugees. That was a working kitchen. That's it, more or less. But if I stayed in the centre late, then I would sleep in one of the hotels there, most often in the Union Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So from time to time you stayed at the Union Hotel. From time to time you were at this refugee centre in Zvezdara.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or I went to the Hotel Moskva.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Hotel Moskva too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you there by yourself? I know that you have a wife. Did you arrive there with your wife or were you by yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was by myself then. My wife was with me for a certain period of time when I was at the medical military hospital, then I transferred her in March to get out of all of that crowded area, but for a brief period of time she stayed with me at the Hotel Moskva where we were together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, when you say March are you talking about 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1991. I'm talking about 1991. This is all 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the fuss in March 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I left the prison hospital, when I came home, there were attempts to attack the house. There were telephone threats, all of these things, and my health wasn't all that good either. However, I could not go for treatment to the city hospital. I had to go to Belgrade, and I was at the Military Medical Academy for a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking this because you said that this was in March. I understood that you were released from prison in Zagreb in April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, April. You are correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked not to overlap because of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I just want to round off this part. So in this period from the 20th of May you were in Belgrade. Were you by yourself or were you with your wife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And your wife remained in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She stayed in my father's or her father's house in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's not clear what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you say that it was your father's or her father's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was her father's house in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, as you are both speaking the same language and that has to be translated, you should try to avoid overlapping. So please wait until you can see that on the screen the translation has finished before you answer the question of Mr. Zivanovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Belgrade? Can you please tell me that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until October. October or November. When the staff in Sid was established, the Territorial Defence Staff, that's when I transferred to Sid. This was in late October, early November. I don't recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And when this Territorial Defence Staff in Sid was formed, you went there, and you slept in Sid practically.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I had a friend in the village of Adasevci in front of Sid as you take the highway. That's where I would sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in your answer to a question by the Prosecutor, you said that for a while you were in Lovas. Can you just tell us when it was exactly that you were staying in Lovas? When did you leave Sid and go to Lovas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't really give you the dates, but when the Tovarnik, the action in Tovarnik and Lovas stopped, when the combat actions in that area stopped, that's when I went to Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If these dates are correct or the approximate time periods, October, November, that means that you went to Lovas after staying in Sid or in this village of Adasevci for a while; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And think that you said that you stayed in Lovas until Vukovar was liberated, when you returned to your house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, Mr. Savic, before you joined the Serbian Democratic Party, you were a member of the League of Communists of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, just like the majority of people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell me why you decided to leave the League of Communists of Croatia and join the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in a single-party system, everyone is a member of the party. That applies to the League of Communists as well. And the main reason is the membership fee, the membership dues. My ideological leanings are not of Communist type. Even in my last term of office, actually, I was at the post of the secretary of the local organisation. When I was appointed secretary of the local organisation, and when I was supposed to give a speech, I said something to this effect: Evidently, the party has reached an end, because a term of office was given to me. That seems to be the end of the party. And I will not regret being the person to dig a grave for the party. So then the other members wanted me to face disciplinary proceedings, and then I said I didn't know of any secretary who had sent himself for a disciplinary procedure. What am I trying to say? For ten years there had been a general crisis in the state, a crisis of Communism, actually. The party had used up all of its credits. It had to hand over power, and it was the most difficult thing for them to do, to hand over or to give up their power. So it was evident that there would be turbulent changes, especially because after the elections in Croatia where the Party of Democratic Action, actually the League of Communists changed its name to the Party of Democratic Changes, party the SDP, and they got the vote of all the Serbs in the elections and then simply left them high and dry. The Serbs were no longer necessary following the elections in a multi-party system. The Serbian Democratic Party was established in Knin. It won seats in the parliament. It became a parliamentary party. Its area of activity was the Republic of Croatia, and in some estimate of mine it seemed logical that we would need to join in these activities. So this is the only reason. There was no major sadness or regret at leaving the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, one thing is odd in this answer of yours. If you were not a person with Communist convictions, why did you have to join the party at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because of the membership dues. Like I said, the party exerts pressure on you to join, because they want you to pay the membership dues. So it wasn't even complicated to join the party. You could do that on the spot in the course of a day, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did that bring any privileges with it perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the privileges went to the political establishment. I was working. I didn't have any political ambitions, and I didn't expect any privileges that would come to me from the party, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But the fact that you accepted to become secretary of the party organisation, I mean, that is an official function after all, particularly in a situation where you don't share those convictions. But on the other hand, would that give you some privileges? Did party secretaries receive any privileges from the Communist Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the party disappeared silently. It was no longer there. After the elections, the party just disappeared from view.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying this because I understood from your answer that the party changed its name and that it was called the League of Communists of Croatia Party of Democratic Changes. So it didn't disappear. It stayed, but it had a modified platform and a different name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the election and the election of the new municipal leadership, the president of the municipality was Slavko Dokmanovic. Slavko Dokmanovic was my colleague who also worked in the Vupik enterprise. I tried to provide a kind of guideline to Slavko Dokmanovic so that his direction of activity would be Zagreb, because a lot of information was already coming from Belgrade data of the intelligence type and so on, but he told me, Nobody wants to receive me in Zagreb. I tried through one of my friends who was a representative in the Croatian Assembly from our list from Vukovar to try to see with Racan whether it was possible for someone to receive him, and he literally told him -- he told me, I went to see Racan. He's making some sort of calculation with 4 million German marks in order to purchase mortars and he said he doesn't want to talk to me. Well, the Communists in any case tacitly transferred their power to the HDZ, and this changeover of power was very quick and very quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1989 or in 1990, but I think that it was in 1989, the multi-party system was introduced in Croatia, so there were a lot of parties. Can you please tell me why was it that you chose the Serbian Democratic Party in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I explained a little bit before what the position of Serbs in Croatia was, especially after the decision to embark on multi-party elections and after the HDZ became active. The party began to spread a very unfavourable climate. There was a lot of fear. They publicly attacked Serbs, and that was the only topic that mobilised the party in the elections that it was participating in. And so when it became an open fear that the Serbs, and it would be -- was quite normal to try to encourage people to get out of the blockade and to try to start thinking in a different way. So I cannot go for the Croatian parties when -- when they don't need me. Perhaps in some normal circumstances that would be possible. I mean, if somebody tells you, I don't need you. You don't need to bother with me, why would I offer myself up to them? So then the natural choice in that situation seemed to be the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said, I think at pages 16 and 17 of today's LiveNote, that you spoke to about 300 or 400 people, that there was fear among them, that they were afraid of political involvement with the Serbian Democratic Party, I assume you meant. I would like to ask you the following question: Who were they really afraid of, or what were they afraid of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that I've shared that with you already. There was a large-scale attack on Serbs by the political leaders of the states. People somehow believed that by not becoming involved, by doing nothing, they would be best protected and eventually saved. It was very difficult to convince people that what was being said was actually true and that these actions would be taken, although just to be perfectly clear about this, I fully understood the strategy of the Croatian Democratic Party, the period that was defined as Croatia's silence, which was roughly the same time as the happening of the people in Serbia, as they called it. This was an interesting moment in time, because Croatia as a country defined its political objective and its general direction for the future, and they said this in no uncertain terms. It's not something they were trying to conceal. They received international support for their goals. They publicly spoke about the fact that they enjoyed the support for their future actions. Those of us living alongside Croats were fully aware of this. We all knew that the Croats wanted an independent state, an independent country, which as a desire was something that I viewed as natural, and I respected that. I said so many times that we were told this in public, so many times, which I appreciated. The only thing I didn't appreciate is those who said they would be standing up for me, defending me. Now, that was something that I couldn't understand. Why would someone defend me and protect me when I needed no defending or protecting. So it was the defenders who actually played a much more prominent role in this than the Croats. Now, we the Serbs, and this is why I fail to understand the policies pursued by Belgrade, the Serbs failed to capture this moment of social change. In a democracy, what really matters is the numbers. They were the largest single group in Yugoslavia, and obviously they would lead any changes, and obviously they would have been the first to organise elections. Why weren't they in pure historical terms? Well that's a different matter altogether, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But that is beyond the scope of my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just trying to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP in 2003, you spoke in detail about these attacks on Serbs. You said that after the 2nd of May and what happened at Borovo Selo, these attacks became more intense. We have information suggesting that Serbs were being fired from their jobs throughout the area, and I think you said that too. Some were even killed, some were threatened, and so on and so forth. Was that the reason that the people you spoke to, the 3- or 400 persons that you mentioned were afraid to get politically involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, an enormous fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you some video footage today, and you were asked about the concept of Ustasha. I know that your family were not in Croatia during the war, and I know that that is not where you hail from originally, but we have information suggesting that among the people who were living there, there were many persons who had very unfortunate memories of that time. I'm talking about World War II, people whose families had been killed by the Ustasha during World War II. I'm sure you've heard of these instances as well, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is certainly true, but I would like to explain something else. That period was never sufficiently clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'd rather we just don't go into that now. We don't want to be explaining this now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but this is something that is abused, so we're looking at an abuse here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Likewise, we heard about people who survived, but they still had these unpleasant memories about the fates met by their families, and our people were wary of this emerging Independent State of Croatia, lest something might happen again, the same sort of thing that happened back in World War II. Did you ever come across people feeling that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did, and I said so, didn't I.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You know that between the two wars, during that time there were some Ustasha organisations, not in Yugoslavia, abroad for the most part. But are you aware that in 1989 or 1990, some members of those organisations arrived back in Croatia and began to organise themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but the Communists were still in power at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The borders were opened up, and all those who wished to go back were free to do so. That's what the propaganda was like at the time. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So we may therefore conclude that groups like that existed in Croatia at the time, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but nobody was even trying to conceal their existence. Everyone knew that those people were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Ustasha groups, is that who you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, all the immigrants come back were labelled as Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Are you trying to control the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There's something else that I would like to ask you. I know that not everyone, not every person who had gone on aboard was an Ustasha and whoever said this was the case was certainly wrong. That is most certainly not the case, but my question is very specific. I'm talking about 1989, 1990. Were there any Ustasha groups in Croatia? I'm talking about groups. I'm not saying that everyone who moved back to Croatia from somewhere else abroad was automatically an Ustasha. I'm asking you about the existence of any groups like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People who had previously lived abroad for a long time were now returning, those who wished to return and those who had good reason for returning. Were they members of a Ustasha organisation or not is not something I can say. When we are talking about immigrants, then let's cover the whole category. Some people came back of their own free will, some were duped into going back, but I think, yes, it would be logical to see the whole thing in terms of people going back, those who wished to go back and were now finally free to go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I hesitate to rise, but this has been happening for the second time now. I think we should be very careful when putting questions to the witness not to give evidence. It is all right to put questions, but comments such as, People were most certainly wrong about this or that position, I think -- I would advise that counsel be careful about not putting his side of the story but putting questions to the witness rather than giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that I could put the leading question to the witness, and I could lead him in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So I wasn't talking about emigres here. You were living in Croatia at the time, and you would have been able to tell. Is that what people said publicly? Were any rallies like that held? That's what my question was about, about the nature of any rallies. I'm not asking you whether somebody who attended a meeting came from abroad or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was my understanding of your question, and that's what determined my answer, but coast was now clear for any organisations that wished to start operating. That much is certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You've just explained that in your understanding the Serbian Democratic Party was operating in Croatia and that was the way it should be. So it should look to Zagreb. Based on your statement, I see that sometime in May 1990, you went to Belgrade to be there for the meeting at which the Serbian Democratic Party was established in Belgrade, so I'm wondering about this opinion of yours. Does this opinion go back to that time or did you form that opinion at later stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Serbian Democratic Party in Knin. It was under the control of the State Security Service in Serbia. The setting up of the board in Belgrade was interpreted as an activity performed by people from the area of Knin, Dalmacija, Lika, and so on and so forth, but living in Belgrade. So that's who the border's being set up for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There's something else that I'd like to know. At the time Yugoslavia was a single country. I don't know if there were any restrictions to the effect that a political party was only allowed to operate in a certain area and not throughout the former country. Hence my question, I assume the meeting in Belgrade was perfectly legal and the Party of Democratic Action was free to set up its own boards wherever it chose to, the same thing that applied to the work of any other political party at the time. Wasn't that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We know what the platform was and that's what I'm telling you. As long as Yugoslavia was single and intact -- there are different interpretations of that to begin with. But it would have been pointless to get Yugoslavia involved. I'm talking about our side, the Serbian Democratic Party. Each newly founded political party has its own territory and ground that it covers. Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you actually say that at the meeting of the Serbian Democratic Party in Belgrade when the Serbia board was established? Did you stand up? Did you speak up that this wasn't right, that this wasn't the way it should be, that the Serbian Democratic Party should only operate in Croatia and that it wasn't right for its board to be established in Belgrade of all places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there as an observer. I had no right to take part in the actual work of the meeting. They followed an agenda with speakers on it, and they had all these things that they would do, but I had no right to be involved in the discussion of that meeting, and that's not what I was after anyway. What I was after was meeting up with Raskovic in order talk to him and see if there was anything that we could do together to enhance the work of our party in Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the first time you met Raskovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You knew that on the 17th of February that same year, the Serbian Democratic Party had been established in Knin and that he was its president, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You knew that party's platform, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you told him at the time that you wanted a board established in Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Slavonia and Baranja. The term "Western Srem" was only mentioned later on, but during our original conversation, we talked about Slavonia and Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know one thing about the platform of the Serbian Democratic Party? Among other things, it talks about the establishment of territorial autonomy. Should that be the option chosen by the population at a referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that all these things about autonomy had to do with how things went elsewhere in Yugoslavia. Would Croatia emerge as an independent country? Would there now be a confederation or a different form of organisation? So the autonomy issue and the right to autonomy very much hinged on these other contiguous developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of a political motto held by Raskovic at the time? He said the number of Serbs in Croatia should be the same as the number of Croats in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember that. It's not a platform. It's probably something that he said at a rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I believe this was misinterpreted. My question was misinterpreted, hence I'll repeat it. Raskovic's motto was Serbs should be in Croatia to the same extent that Croatia is in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this is probably something that he exclaimed at a public rally or something like that. It wasn't a proper political platform. But there's one thing I would like to add if I may. We are in no position to impose an ultimatum on Croatia. Croatia as a country had its own constitution, its own laws, and it was supposed to make room for others too. If it denied some political rights to the Serbs, then they had to include the Serbs in some other category. Okay. So ethnic minority was the category chosen. The status of an ethnic minority might be debatable, but amid all the chaos that reigned at the time, it was the way in which this was done that was perceived as particularly humiliating. Nevertheless, the times being what they were, there was nothing much you could do about it. You had to wait for the whole thing to calm down a little, and we had to wait for a better moment, a better time to discuss these things in circumstances that were back to normal. That's why we were in no position to impose an ultimatum on Croatia as a country. This is how you see us, so this is what we'll do back to you. No, that was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell me this, please: What do you mean when you say when better times come, a better moment? That's what you said, something to that effect, better circumstances. Which circumstances would that be, because on one hand you have Croatia seeking independence, secession from Yugoslavia. On the other hand, you have Serbs in Croatia who don't want that. So what would be these better times that were supposed to come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, there was a clash between two concepts and between two types of people, those who saw a solution of that chaotic situation within a legal framework and those who saw that solution through the use of any type of ammunition, as powerful as possible. That would be it put simply. That's what the conflict was about. That's what everything resolved around. But in a situation that was so chaotic, for you to define your political goals and your rights was impossible. Our position should have been to work to reach a legal framework. Of course the Serbs did not accept the state as it was. They had their rights. They had their property within their own state, so who was saying that they were not wanted in at that state? First of all, let's see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say the following: That there was a problem, that the problem should have been resolved through legal means but that there were people who were misusing that? Are you saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, also the separation within the state should have been resolved by legal means, because in a -- in a situation where a state is trying to split up, there are no legal solutions for such a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question before the break. Are you aware that in a referendum the Serbs voiced their position on the secession of Croatia from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I implemented that referendum in Vukovar. In the building, in the office in the centre of town was where that referendum was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is not what I was asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I will tell you now. I simply have no confidence in referendums whose results are 98 or 99 per cent in favour. That would be my answer to your question. Who initiated the whole holding of the referendum, and why was this done? In any case, we did a hundred crazy tasks which were imposed on us regarding political rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, can you just tell me this: You have already said that you voiced your distrust in relation to such a referendum.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The one that was implemented by the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, can you -- yes, yes. I'm just going to tell you one more thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question and then we will finish before the break. And you, at that time, did not leave the Serbian Democratic Party even though in a way you knew and you asserted that this referendum was not proper, that the results of the referendum were not accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not a person who gives up. I just follow the manipulation as it develops, and I'm aware of the manipulation that somebody would impose on me, but I have to do something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can have a break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Savic, we will take the second break now and come back at 5.15. You will be escorted out of the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: While the -- while the witness is brought in -- while the witness is brought in, we have a short oral ruling to put on the record. It's about joint motion seeking admission of agreed documents. On the 19th of October, 2012, the Prosecution and the Defence filed a joint motion seeking admission of 56 documents. One document designed as Rule -- designated - sorry - as Rule 65 ter number 00809 has already been admitted as Exhibit L3. The Chamber finds that the remaining documents are relevant and have probative value and shall be admitted and marked. The Registry is directed to assign exhibit numbers beginning with P and L as outlined in the motion. The Chamber notes that there was a typographical error in Annex A to the motion and the document listed as ordinal number 12 should have Rule 65 ter 00358.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Savic, I wanted to put one more question to you about your stay in Serbia after the 2nd of May, 1991. Are you able to tell me what you did when you were in Odzaci? What were you doing? What were you busy with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosko Perosevic was the president of the municipality in Odzaci. We knew one another. We tried to organise assistance for the refugees, and in co-operation with him and Brana Crncevic, that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what did this assistance or aid comprise? Specifically, what is it that you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was trying to bring in medicines. Look, everybody knew me. I received a truck full of medicines from the Sabac pharmaceutical industry, for example. There was help from the municipality of Zrenjanin and other neighbouring municipalities. And then we transferred that across to Borovo, and since we had medical solutions from Sabac, we would provide the hospitals along -- that to the hospitals by the -- using the Danube River. This is more or less what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, you were collecting medicines and other types of assistance in Serbia and then you were sending it to Borovo and other parts of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also, we were sending it to centres that were receiving refugees. For example, there was certain schools along the Danube River bank where they were receiving refugees. For example, there was a location in Vajska, and we gave this help there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May, 1991, when you went there, I don't think that there were any refugees in Serbia. The war hadn't started then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had already starting appearing after the 2nd of May. We had a ferry in Borovo Selo, something that I arranged with Novakovic, because there they were working with small boats, but we obtained a proper ferry, and the wave of refugees already was beginning to cross over the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what was your reason to move to Belgrade? I think you said that you went there sometime in June or after the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I didn't feel safe, personally, in Odzaci. One morning at approximately 7.00 a.m. somebody began to knock on my door. My neighbour said, You left your car. You parked it and it was in the way. But when I come to the building, I always park in a place where I don't bother anyone. I let the water run in the toilet in the bathroom, and I said, I'm having a shower. I will come down shortly, come downstairs. And I took a shower, I got my things, and after a certain period of time I went out, went to my car, and I went to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And so you didn't go back there to sleep, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And this thing that your neighbour said, you took that as some sort of threat against you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. I had very, very sharp instincts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On three occasions in your statement, and you didn't mention this, but in your statement you mention three times that you were supposed to be killed. I can read that part of your statement back to you. This is paragraph 171. You said that this happened that day when a body -- when the body of Vukasin Soskocanin was taken out of the Danube River, and you said that this was ordered by Milosevic, that this Kertes was supposed to carry this out and that Ljubo Novakovic was an accomplice in all of this. Well, we know who Milosevic is, but can you explain to us what Kertes was doing? Who was he at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kertes was always God. He was a man who was a close associate of Slobodan Milosevic. He was involved in everything that had to do with personnel policy in the area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. He was involved in all issues of any kind of assistance whatsoever, and he controlled that area, simply speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have information that at that time he was assistant of the federal minister of the interior. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I agree. It's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And Ljubo Novakovic, who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ljubo Novakovic was the president of the Backa Palanka municipality. To us the municipality was a place to meet. Goran would stop by there, Vukasin. Everybody from the area would come by. That's where our meeting place was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you managed to avoid this because you didn't go to the bank of the Danube River, which you said in your statement. Instead you went to Odzaci; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So if you can explain to me how do you explain the fact that such powerful people at the time, Milosevic as the president of the state at the time, Kertes's assistant, Ministry of the Interior and as you said God for that area, do not carry out what was planned, this alleged murder against you and that you managed just to evade that by going away and leaving, going some 10 kilometres farther?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I always had more information. The way in which Vukasin Soskocanin was liquidated was something that I was familiar with. I know that the divers attached him to a -- a piece of wood, a log, and he could not float up. So at a meeting that Kertes was presiding over, he asked me to give my support to him, because there were about 50 people from that area. They were talking about arms sales and for this to be settled. At the beginning of the meeting, Trifun Ivkovic came in from Sremska Mitrovica he was, and I don't need to repeat what is in my statement. Trifun Ivkovic is a major provocateur, and you always have to analyse the things he says and does between the lines. The fact is that I didn't want to be a president, and I didn't want to be involved in anything. And then he asked the question, Why is Goran the president when we agreed that it should be Boro? In the meantime Ljuba Novakovic brought a paper to me on which it said that near Novo Selo, this is a village right on the bank of the Danube River, a body has floated up, and so that I should go and see to check if that's Vukasin Soskocanin. So what would you think after something like that? I told Kertes, All right. I'm leaving now. And I told Ljuba, I don't have a car. And he said, Well, my driver will take you. And so when we set off, I told him, You drive me to Odzaci. And the police was already there on the left bank of the Danube, and the executors of the act were together with the police. I am not guessing, but that is the way. This is how they get rid of people. Why would I go and check something that I know for a fact was impossible? Well, that's my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time you mentioned the fact that the perpetrators were there on the riverbank. The perpetrators of what exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The perpetrators or the executors of death penalties. It wasn't about swimming, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you have been sentenced to death by someone from that group you refer to. Okay. And now these people are here, and they are supposed to execute your sentence. Is that what you're talking about when you say "perpetrators"? Mr. Savic, you were driven to Odzaci by Ljubo Novakovic's driver; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He probably said where he drove you to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I told him to say that, Tell Ljubo that you dropped me off at Odzaci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, if you would allow -- you seemed to ask the witness: "In other words, you have been sentenced to death by someone from that group you refer to. Okay. And now these people are here and they are supposed to execute you -- your sentence. Is that what you're talking about when you say 'perpetrators?'" And then without asking for -- without waiting for an answer, you go about: "Where you were driven to Odzaci by Novakovic's driver; right?" So now I'm -- aren't we missing something here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: When you say: "In other words, you have been sentenced to death," do you mean the witness or do you mean a person in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I mean about the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That the witness was sentenced to death. It was his testimony as far as I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat the question: Did you say that you were, as a matter of fact, sentenced to death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's my assessment, which I believe to be correct, and that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And these perpetrators were there in order to execute you, to carry out this death sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We'd be speculating, wouldn't we. But why else would they want me to go to the riverbank? Listen, I'm not paranoid. My anti-war activity was very unpopular. Even the government -- when the government was set up for Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, they banned [Realtime transcript read in error "banded"] all of their members from talking to me. I knew what this was about, and this wasn't the first time I faced a situation like that, starting with Plitvice and you can take it from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is precisely what I wanted to ask you. How do you explain the fact that these perpetrators were there to carry out your own death sentence on the banks of the Danube. How come they didn't drive over to Odzaci later on, because they knew that you were there. It's a well known fact. It was known to Ljubo Novakovic, for example, who you define as one of the people involved, an accomplice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was still not a time of large-scale executions, which is what came later on as the conflict escalated. It's about taking advantage of someone's gullibility, getting that person killed as smoothly and as trouble free as possible. I can tell you how they liquidated Soskocanin. It is not a subject that is unfamiliar to me. It's not something that I couldn't cope with.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I have a small intervention for the transcript, Mr. Zivanovic. At page 73, line 6, when the witness says, "when the government was set up for Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, they banned," I think the word "banned" is misspelled there. I just wanted to put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you were banned or forbidden in terms of communicating with the members of the government. It's about the interpretation. That's why I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was banned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now that we have come to that, in paragraph 191 of your statement, and if that's required, I can always go back to the original text if you want me to. You can see it on your screen too. It's 5868. You said you were on a list of persons to be killed. This was ordered by the service, and the government members were banned from contacting you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A list. Okay. I did not see a list. Banned from contacting me, that's what the government members themselves told me, you see. The way in which persons were selected to be liquidated, I don't know. Maybe that too is an interpretation matter. So -- list. I wouldn't say me, a list, no. But it's a fact that all those who opposed the way in which the area was operating - I'm talking about Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem and the area right across the Danube - all those were undesirable in terms of staying there. They didn't want them there any more. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But at the time you weren't in the area, were you, when the government was set up, if I understand you correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody in that area knows me. It doesn't matter if I'm physically there at a certain point in time or not. Do you understand that? I had lots of contacts with people from across the river starting with the municipal presidents, Backa Palanka, Sombor, factory managers, doctors, lawyers. I would practice once a month. We would meet at Banja Junakovic more often than not. And then we would meet there, then I would explain to them at these meetings how they could best help us. So I was co-ordinating. This was about co-ordinating different tasks. So to come back to this, it's an area in which I'm a familiar face. In anybody wants to know anything, if there's anything they need to raise, they get in touch with me. They ask the question. As for me physically staying in that area, because this is what I'm talking about, and where else should I go after all?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said the government members told you that any contact with you was banned. Can you specify which government members told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bogdan Vorkapic was one of them. I think he was the economy minister, something like that. Milos Vojnovic was another. He was the justice minister. He was a nice lad. Our relations were great. And that's all I remember. But I don't think it takes more people than that. It's quite enough if one person says it. I hadn't even known about this, but I met Bogdan Vorkapic in Belgrade at Terazije. I was about to ask him a question and there he was running away from me and I said, Bogdan, hold it right there. I want to ask you a question. And he says literally, Listen, I'm sorry, but I'm not allowed to talk to you. It's not that I was necessarily greatly taken aback by this. I said, Okay. Fine. Let it be, if that's the way it is. It's not that I was pressing him or anything. I wasn't actively seeking contact anymore after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He and this other man, Vojnovic, did they perhaps tell you that your name was marked for liquidation, that the service ordered your killing, in other words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Why would I ask them such a question? And it's not really something that they would have been told anyway. They are just doing their jobs, and this is something external. It was extraneous to their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So who was it that told you about the fact the service had ordered you to be killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I told you my instincts were alive and well. It's not that I went rummaging about or asking questions, you see. I wasn't nosing around. It was just the general impression I got based on my contacts with different people. I knew how far I was allowed to go, but there is no need to insist on this point. There's no need to push this point. It's just something that my instinct told me, and I tried to steer clear. This was nothing that stood out at the time, nothing particularly special.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 180, of your statement, you also say that you were informed in July 1991 by Djordje Bozovic, also known as Giska --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, just in case you're moving to another topic, we have heard several times that the discussion was about the service, the service having ordered this, and having banned -- I suppose, banned the witness as well. Could we clarify with the witness which service we are talking about just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Savic, you make numerous references also in the paragraph that I just mentioned and elsewhere in your statement to "the service." Could you please be more specific about what this means. What do you mean by "the service"? What is the context for that particular usage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the only service that I could possibly mean in this context were that being the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The State Security Service of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbia. That's what we're talking about, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 180 of your statement, you say that in July 1991, Djordje Bozovic, also known as Giska, offered to help you if you ever felt threatened in Belgrade, and then one night he warned you that you should escape because there were threats coming from Hadzic, he suggested, but your take on it was that the threats actually originated from Knin, the people in Knin. So the first thing that I wish to clarify, if you look at this paragraph, you'll see a reference there to a man named Borcevic. Is that the same person or is this a typing mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Djordje Bozovic. I think that's who we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So that's the same person, Djordje Bozovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did that person perhaps tell you anything about why you were encountering these difficulties, why you were receiving threats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Giska was the commander of the volunteer brigade belonging to the SPO. He was one of the state perpetrators, so to speak, as well as Arkan, Martic, and the others. I asked him why he wasn't with Arkan. Since they had this guard, why wasn't he with them. And he said, They're all Communists over there, and I had no business being with then. When I came to Belgrade after Plitvice, I told you about my instinct; right? I have feelings, you know. I know that the way I pursued my own peace mission was at odds with the historical moment. So I pleaded with him. I said, You're moving about in these circles. I have to tell you, I'm not feeling particularly safe in Belgrade. I don't have anybody in particular that I can name, but I assume we're talking about a certain type of people who are in the know, you know, and they exchange a lot of info. So you see, you're actually the only guy around here that I trust so I'm telling you this. Just let me know. No need to ask any further. Everything after that is up to me. I was sleeping at the union, and he came about 10.00. He said, Listen, bro, because that's how we talked to each other, he said, Get up. Get ready to leave. You've got to be off this very minute. Do you want me to go on or -- so I said to him, Who is this from? He said, Goran. And I said, Well, you know what? I don't buy it for a minute. It's not Goran, but okay. There are all sorts of people doing all sorts of things here, but all I can do is the next morning first thing I'll check what this is about. And he said, I'll stay with you till next morning, and we did, as a matter of fact. I left for Matica that morning to see Brana Crncevic. Brana Crncevic and I were sitting in the same office. Actually, I was sitting in his office. And I said, Could you please call Radmilo. I want to talk to him. So Radmilo showed up in no time at all. The shortest time possible it would have taken him to get there from the government building. So he realised that we knew each other. So this was a man I trusted and there was nothing I couldn't share with him. So we greeted each other and he said, Well, where have you been? What's up? And I said, Listen, aren't you surprised to see me still alive, and he said, Well, what on earth do you mean? And then I told him the whole story about what transpired and then he said, I know nothing about that. I really can't confirm. Be that as it may, if there's anything that needs doing, I'll give you hand. So that was that. And then I told him, Listen, I have three lawyers in Belgrade. I have left my materials and documents evenly distributed with these three. So no matter who ends up being the one doing it, these lawyers have my permission to use these materials and actually publish them. So that's how the whole thing ended in the roughest of terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned this material. Can you please tell me whether the material refers specifically to these events which could then present some sort of danger to you? Is that something that happened in 1990 or 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's just a bluff. There was no material at all. However, in that situation, you know what it means to publish something. And even if you say that you have something, people think that you do have it, you know? So, well, you know, there's a saying that depending on the market, the goods are like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So in this period from the 2nd of May until June, your life was in danger, you're saying, from members of the security service. Is that what you're saying? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's assume that. Actually, I assumed that. I don't know as to what sort of service it was. I mean, there were many of those who were there for liquidations. I mean, there were some informal condemnations to death, not just from the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the reasons for that were your political beliefs or your opposition at the time to the policies that were implemented in Yugoslavia or Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was spreading anti-war ideas, and would I always say that the Croats have the right to do what they're doing, and then they would say, Well, what are you talking about the Croats? And I would say, Well, they have the right to do that. Why are you bothering me with Croats and it's a fact that we're there and we're not in Croatia. Why don't you clean up your own house first? That was more or less what I said. I'm not somebody who would keep quiet. I would tend to provoke discussions from -- with people. So that's what the discussion and the stories were about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, you know that in 1991, there were many opponents of Slobodan Milosevic's policies; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You know that on the 9th of March, 1991, there were major demonstrations which were attended by over 100.000 people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But there were many more who respected his policies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean at the demonstrations or are you saying generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally speaking. Those who had power in their hands would determine the direction that things were moving in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that in those demonstrations there were many political parties participating from Serbia at the time and these parties had many followers. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to me? You see, I don't know at that any of the people who took part in the demonstrations, the leaders of those parties, those prominent figures who had a large number of followers. I don't know that any of them were killed either by Milosevic or by any of those secret services. So I wanted to ask you what was your reason for believing that the regime was so angry at you? You didn't have an army behind you or a political party. You didn't have a large number of followers and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that I rated highly enough for something like that, but they did acknowledge that in the area where I worked I did have a certain amount of influence, that I had a large number of people who trusted me to whom I did not lie and with whom I didn't play any politics. In that area, I still have people. Many of my friends paid with their heads because of that. This is why I withdrew, because of the people who trusted me. I told them, Don't touch any of these people any more. So you cannot really compare the political scene in Belgrade. This is something that is co-ordinated and done. All of those parties at one point in time were in the opposition, and at one point became the organs of power, but they all had the same master. The League of Communists split into a lot of parties, but they did it in such a way that everybody was ours. I mean, if you look at Vuk Draskovic, did he do better because he was just beaten instead of being killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to deal with what you said about Draskovic in any way, but I wanted something else now. You just said that you told someone, Don't touch them. Who did you say this to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that to Radmilo Bogdanovic at the time when we were sitting at Brana's: Please don't touch people who trust me. I am getting out of all of this. I am not interested in this. You can reach Vienna if you want, wherever you like, but I'm no longer interested in any of this. I always had contacts with whomever I wanted to, and in Belgrade they would always tell me that all the doors were open to me, but I didn't go to any of these doors. You understand. So like I said, I'm not a paranoid person and so on, but it's quite normal in certain circumstances to think about oneself, and this is not something that should dwell on a lot. That's what the circumstances were like at the time. I managed to come out of all of that. This is not some major topic for discussion, you know, but I left Belgrade and went to Sid because it was not safe for me in Belgrade anymore. Then I left Sid, then I went to Lovas because it was not safe for me in Sid anymore. Simply this was my assessment. That's how I was moving, you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you spoke with Radmilo Bogdanovic and that you said this to him, not to touch these people who shared your beliefs. Is this something that he was intending to do? Was it your impression that -- I thought that he came to your summons because you felt threatened that night.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In any case, Radmilo Bogdanovic was a person whom I trusted. I already said that. So when I tell him something, I expect in view of his range of activities and his people and everything, I tell him so if there's any need for anything further. Let him explain, you understand? I don't think that he's the one doing all of this, and leading in all these matters, but he has a broad circle of people, so it's something that should be put through their ears. I mean, it's not something that was specifically aimed in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us here that you went to Sid in late October sometime, I think, and that you sheltered in Sid because you felt threatened in Belgrade. Before you left for Sid, did you have any threats or was there any reason for you to feel in danger from anyone or anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Matica had a warehouse in Belgrade at the fair where the assistance was collected and passed on. I was working on that, and a lot of our people from the Slavonia area were working there. Since weapons and weaponry was also sent out from that warehouse, I didn't get involved in that. Simply people were doing that. And they, those people who were dealing with that, were in contact with the services, and they would be regularly reporting back to me what was going on, who was coming and going without any major insistence on my part. And at one time I was at the -- in the warehouse and a friend came by and he said, A friend wants to see you. All right. Let's get in the car. We went to the Knez Mihajlova Street. I don't know which number, but it was a different building from the federal SUP building when you enter. Actually, it was the Knez Milosa Street, not the Knez Mihajlova Street. And I went to these premises and colonel, a colonel appeared, Colonel Djokovic, who at the time was the deputy chief of the Military Intelligence Service KOS. It was some sort of stage like that. So we greeted each other. We introduced one -- ourselves and he said, You don't have to say anything to me. I know everything. Meaning we don't have time. There's no time for nothing. And he said, Tell me what you are intending to do. I said, I'm not intending to do anything. I'm waiting for the fighting to stop and then I am going home. And he said, Well, do you know that you cannot go there? You're not allowed to go there. You mustn't go there. I said, Well, all right. Then you know that I will go. If you know that I am not allowed to go there, then you know that I will also go there. And he said to me, Listen, the only thing that I can help you with -- well, do you have any weapons? I said, No, I don't. He said, The only thing I can help you with is to give you weapons. What are you going to do with the weapons? I said, Look, I don't have any weapons. I don't want to have anything to do with that, and if I did receive any weapons it would only be with an accompanying permit. And he said, All right, what do you want? There was a large number of things on offer and I said, All right, just give me a Skorpion. I mean, I didn't know much about it but a Skorpion was a status symbol, so I received this Skorpion. He said, Well, I don't have any ammunition but you can get some at the fair. Take a box. And so what I was supposed to do? They were controlling everything. Was I supposed to ask him what all this was about, what was going on? You understand? General Nenezic, whom I used to visit at his home and we would meet regularly, he always used to say to me, Be careful, you're being followed. He is an old KOS person. He knows all these principles. My car was broken into in front of the Sumatovac. My bag was taken, my files, everything that was in the car. Everything that was inside. So what was I supposed to check further? I don't have time or any need to check anything. I have my own path and I have an instinct that guides me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And when you received this Scorpion you went to Sid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After a couple of days. After a couple of days there was something like this that a staff was being formed in Sid and that they were going to commit a massacre, that they were going to push people there to get killed. That was the assessment of General Nenezic. I told him, Listen, I will go to Sid and I came to Sid with only one sole objective and that was to try to prevent some major casualties from occurring or from some put up conflicts or clashes from breaking out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, what was General Nenezic? What was his rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was retired. He was retired. However, every Friday he would go to see Milosevic. Well, I don't know Milosevic had a couple of these generals in an advisory role. I don't know exactly. Well, for consultations and things like that, and he told me openly, You know this is not some kind of mystique surrounding this whole area. So when this -- when I was there when he would come back from Milosevic, he would call me and then he would tell me everything that was discussed. And on one occasion he came and he told me the Vozd, the ruler is very dissatisfied. The situation is not very good at all and then he mentioned all the problems, the situation, and then he said and I told him that I have a man who can resolve these matters. I'm literally retelling you the conversation between us. There was no influence on my behalf, no urging or anything like that. And then when he asked who, I told him about you, and he just laughed and didn't say anything. And he would always stress to me, I always treat you as my protege but I never push you. It's your decision whether you want to do something or not. So these were my relationships with people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you have this conversation with General Nenezic before you went to Sid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, before I went to Sid. I cannot give you an exact date. I simply couldn't remember everything, dates, you know. But this was just before. After that, I went to see General Simovic. Are you interested in --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You talked about that in your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to take your time, but I can just continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when you talked with General Nenezic, do you remember how old he was, what is his state of health?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was an elderly man. And he wasn't in the best of health. However, he was very down and he was very much affected by the situation. He was very unhappy because of the situation in the region, and he always used to say all the people that I had contacts with, yes, they were members of the party, but they were not Communists. He would always be saying, Why are they still holding on to these Communists? They are an anathema to the whole world but they're still propagating these political beliefs and trying to spread them. This is what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When General Nenezic said that in this alleged conversation with Milosevic that he had a person who could resolve the situation and suggested yourself, do you know what he was thinking of? In what way could you resolve the situation? General Nenezic knew some of your positions your views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So are you able to tell us how was it exactly that you were supposed to resolve the situation then in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I have to go back to General Simovic and then that would be the answer to this. And then he asked me he said, Do you want to go to General Simovic? The agreement was that he should be in charge of the cadre policy for that area. Of course I cannot refuse him everything. I said, All right, I will, and he was even surprised. And he said, You really want to? I said, Yes, in an hour I'm going to be at General Simovic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. Why was he surprised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I never wanted nobody and I never wanted to listen to anybody and he was really pleasantly surprised. And I already told you that in the end I actually agreed to do that only because of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment. Since we're already on this topic, in other words, he didn't even expect that you would accept something like that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. I set aside that hour on purpose to prepare the situation at General Simovic's, and I know. I will explain my reasons. So in one hour I was in front of the government building, and I came to General Simovic directly to his desk without any controls. I mean even the door was open.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just for the transcript, could you please tell us what was General Simovic's position at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the defence minister, the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Of Serbia or of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the FR Yugoslavia, Yugoslavia. But actually he, a sinner, wanted to make a Serbian Army while he was in the post of the minister of defence of the Yugoslavia, but this is a different situation. General Simovic was sitting at his desk surrounded by a lot of papers. There was a conference table behind him of some 10 to 12 chairs and there was a person sitting at the table and he said to me, In 15 minutes I have to send a report to the president, so can you please talk to this man here. I told him, General, sir, I came to talk to you, and if you don't have time, I'm sorry, but I don't have time either. The gentleman who was sitting behind him said to me, How can you be talking to the General like that? I said, I'm sorry, I was very polite, I don't know what your role is here. He said, Well, I'm his adjutant. I said, I'm sorry, but adjutants are not at my level. And then he said, You think that we don't know what it is that you want. It's all clear to us. I told him, Look, listen --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting, but when he said, What it is that you want, did he mean you personally or a group that you were representing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He meant me personally. Let me explain. This person was Zvonko, Milosevic's advisor. Milosevic had two advisors. Well, fine leave it be. I'll remember later on. It was a person from Kosovo. And I said to him, You know something? I'm surprised frankly you know what everybody else wants you just don't know what it is you want yourself. So I stood up and left. As simple as that. Having conducted a conversation like that, do you think you can be entirely safe? Secondly, within that one hour that I was there Milosevic had dispatched Zvonko his advisor to be there, and there wasn't much that I could offer. I was always one to offer solutions, but simple ones. It -- it wasn't about any great mysteries, you know. These are matters that could have been resolved after talking for no more than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But could you please share that with us? What exactly did you tell General Nenezic so that he then put your name forward to Milosevic as the man who could take care of the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not that I told him anything. He knew the whole situation. He knew all the people there, what they were doing, where they were going. It's not like he needed me to tell him or indeed to advise him. He was looking into those things. He knew. The KOS has a thousand different services. It's hard to tell them apart. It's hard to know who's doing what. Who knows. But every day the KOS, every morning receives a report from the people out in the field. Colonel Djokovic gets these reports submitted every day, local reports, about certain localities so he reads these and I'm able to guess the actual locations for each and every one of these reports and he said, You're totally insane. How can you know these things? And I said, Well, I know the situation. But one thing that I can tell you is they had all the info. They knew exactly what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not information that I had in mind. I was more wondering about the solutions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But you're asking me why did he do that and how could he know that. It was based on the information that he had and that's what he based his recommendation on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll not discuss this at length because we know about these events at Plitvice. We know about your arrest and Goran Hadzic's arrest on the 1st of March, 1991. We know that the Croatian police gave you very rough treatment, both you and Goran Hadzic, and both of you were actually injured as a result of the treatment you received on the hands of the Croatian police. What I want to know is did you receive any treatment for those injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were not arrested at Plitvice. What you call an arrest was not really an arrest. We were ID'd. I told them who we were and what we were doing, and they clearly said to us that we were the target of their attack. I had been listening in on the co-ordination conducted by the police officers on the one hand and the centre on the other, and at one point the centre asked that we should be sent back. It was a decision taken by someone or other, and we said, Okay, let's be off a bit sooner. So this was mistreatment, mistreatment of which I was the target. And Goran Hadzic could tell, because they said, Don't touch this guy, touch the fat one, the other one over there, which I found a bit ridiculous but there you go. I was able to neutralise any consequences of this attack because I was mentally prepared for this you see. All this harassment, all these blows that I received, all I was trying to do was to remain standing and remain conscious. It was -- in the morning it was cold so I was trying to take in as much oxygen as I could with my mouth wide open. So I did all of this preemptively to do what I could to withstand.
